title: Diagnosing a muddy vocal
canonical_user_question: Why does my vocal sound muddy, and what should I test first?
natural_language_variants: My vocal sounds cloudy and hard to understand.
There is too much low-mid stuff in my vocal.
The voice feels covered by a blanket.
How do I clean up a muddy lead vocal without making it thin?
clarification_questions: Does the problem exist on the raw vocal with every plug-in bypassed?
Is it obvious when the vocal is soloed, or mainly when the full mix plays?
Does it happen throughout the performance or only on certain notes, vowels, or consonants?

candidate_hypotheses.label: H1: Proximity effect or room buildup
candidate_hypotheses.evidence_needed: A current raw and processed capture, plus whether the problem occurs solo and in the full mix.
candidate_hypotheses.discriminating_test: Change or bypass only the stage/source that would create this cause and compare at matched loudness.

candidate_hypotheses.label: H2: Too much low-mid energy in the source
candidate_hypotheses.mechanism: too much low-mid energy in the source
candidate_hypotheses.evidence_needed: A current raw and processed capture, plus whether the problem occurs solo and in the full mix.
candidate_hypotheses.discriminating_test: Change or bypass only the stage/source that would create this cause and compare at matched loudness.

candidate_hypotheses.label: H3: Reverb or compression sustaining low mids
candidate_hypotheses.mechanism: reverb or compression sustaining low mids
candidate_hypotheses.evidence_needed: A current raw and processed capture, plus whether the problem occurs solo and in the full mix.
candidate_hypotheses.discriminating_test: Change or bypass only the stage/source that would create this cause and compare at matched loudness.

candidate_hypotheses.label: H4: Masking from guitars, keys, or bass

recommended_first_experiment.summary: Compare the vocal soloed and in the full mix, then make a small broad temporary low-mid cut only if the mud exists in solo.
recommended_first_experiment.why_this_first: It separates a source, processing, or mix-interaction problem before committing to a permanent EQ curve.
recommended_first_experiment.action: Compare the vocal soloed and in the full mix, then make a small broad temporary low-mid cut only if the mud exists in solo.

logic_pro_steps: Loop the shortest phrase where the problem is obvious.
Bypass the vocal processing chain, or bypass one plug-in at a time, while keeping perceived loudness as close as possible.
Open Channel EQ from the vocal channel strip EQ area or Audio FX > Equalizers > Channel EQ.
Make only the temporary diagnostic move described below; toggle the band or plug-in off and on in the full mix.
Return the control to its previous state before testing a competing explanation.
starting_points: Start with a broad bell and a small cut; sweep slowly through roughly the low-mid region rather than jumping to a fixed frequency.
Match loudness closely when toggling the change; louder is easily mistaken for better.
what_to_listen_for: Words should become easier to follow while the chest and warmth remain intact.
Check the vocal in the full arrangement, then briefly in solo to identify side effects.
stop_rule: Stop or back off as soon as too much cutting makes the vocal thin or hollow.
undo_or_reset: Bypass or delete the temporary EQ band, restore the previous plug-in state, and compare against the raw capture.
rationale: The word “muddy” describes a perception, not a measured cause. The first job is to discover whether the source, processing, or surrounding arrangement produces it.
tradeoffs_and_risks: Too much cutting makes the vocal thin or hollow.
A visually impressive EQ curve is not evidence that the vocal improved.
alternatives_if_wrong: Re-record a short phrase with a changed mic position or delivery when the source itself is the cause.
Adjust the competing instrument or arrangement when the vocal is fine solo but fails in the mix.
Use phrase-specific automation or dynamic control when the issue occurs only intermittently.
common_mistakes: Sweeping a very loud narrow boost and then leaving an extreme cut.
Changing EQ, compression, saturation, and reverb simultaneously.
teaching_principle: A production adjective is a clue. Use one reversible test to identify the cause before prescribing the processor.
do_not_assume: The adjective “muddy” maps to one universal frequency.
A spectral peak proves the listener's complaint.
The vocal itself is at fault when the issue may be masking.
